shell.name: Shell
shell.full: Michelle "Shell" Tee, who runs the pass

dev.name: Dev Null
dev.full: Dev Null, in the dish pit

root.name: Regina Root
root.full: Regina Root, of the Lakeside Ledger

shifts.title: Family Meal
shifts.lesson: Commands: ls, cat, head and wc

intro.text: Look who's back! Ash Bourne, out of the fanciest kitchen in the country, come home to save the family sandwich shop.
I'm here to cook, Uncle Awk. Where are tonight's orders?
In my head! Where they have been for thirty years!
intro.say: [shouting, proud] In my head! Where they have been for thirty years!

intro.text: They're in a file, Chef. I've been typing them up behind his back. Michelle Tee, I run the pass. Everybody calls me Shell.
Here's how this kitchen talks now. You say a command. The kitchen does exactly that and nothing else. It doesn't guess.
Yes, Shell.

brief.text: Start in the walk-in. Ask what files we've got. One word does it.

tickets.hint: One chip: ls lists what's there.

after.text: ls. Short for list. Two files: the menu, and tonight's orders.
after.say: L S. Short for list. Two files: the menu, and tonight's orders.

brief.text: Now read me tonight's orders. All of them, top to bottom.

tickets.hint: cat, then the file you want read out.

after.text: A command, then what to work on. cat is short for concatenate. Nobody has said the long word since 1971.

brief.text: The first three are getting cold. Read me those. Only those.

tickets.hint: head, then -n 3 to say how many, then the file.

after.text: That -n 3 is an option. A dash and a letter, and the command does its one job a little differently.
after.say: That dash N three is an option. A dash and a letter, and the command does its one job a little differently.

brief.text: Family meal's in ten and I need a count. How many orders on the rail? Don't read them to me. I want a number.

tickets.hint: wc counts. -l tells it to count lines.

after.text: wc, for word count. With -l it counts lines. Seven orders, and it even says whose.
after.say: W C, for word count. With dash L it counts lines. Seven orders, and it even says whose.

outro.text: Seven! I could have told you seven!

shifts.title: The Rail
shifts.lesson: grep: keep only the lines you want

intro.text: Dinner. The rail's full, and you don't want to read all of it every time somebody shouts.
I want the beef. Just the beef.
Then you want grep. Give it a word, and it hands back only the lines with that word on them.
Grep! What kind of a word is grep?
A real one, Chef. It's older than the wiring in this building.

brief.text: Beef station wants to know what it owes. Every order with beef on it.

tickets.hint: grep, the word to look for, then the file.

after.text: The word first, then the file. Swap them round and it goes looking for a file called beef.

brief.text: The flat-top just died. No melts till Dev fixes it. Read me everything that ISN'T a melt.
brief.say: The flat-top just died. No melts till Dev fixes it. Read me everything that isn't a melt.

tickets.hint: -v turns grep inside out: the lines without the word.

after.text: Flat-top's fixed. Don't ask what was in it.

brief.text: Uncle Awk writes his notes at whatever volume he's feeling. Find every note that says hot, loud or quiet.

tickets.hint: -i tells grep not to care about capitals.

after.text: I write loud so people LISTEN!
after.say: [shouting] I write loud so people listen!

brief.text: Last call on beef. How many beef orders? Don't read them to me. Count them.

tickets.hint: -c makes grep count the lines instead of printing them.

after.text: Three. Same command, one small option, a different answer. That's most of what there is to know about options.

outro.text: It's quiet. Why is it quiet?
Because nobody is shouting the rail across the room, Chef.

intro.text: Here's the part your fancy kitchen was built on, Chef. The pass.
One station plates. The next one picks it up.
On the line it's this bar: a pipe. Whatever the command on its left prints, the command on its right is handed, instead of a file.
So nobody talks to anybody?
Everybody does one thing and passes it down, Chef. It's the quietest way there is to get a lot done.

brief.text: The health inspector wants to know how many files are in the walk-in. ls lists them. wc -l counts lines. Put the pass between.
brief.say: The health inspector wants to know how many files are in the walk-in. L S lists them. W C dash L counts lines. Put the pass between.

tickets.hint: ls, then the pipe, then wc -l to count what ls printed.

after.text: ls never knew anybody was counting. wc never knew where the lines came from. That's the whole idea.
after.say: L S never knew anybody was counting. W C never knew where the lines came from. That's the whole idea.

brief.text: Two beef, on the fly! The first two beef orders on the rail, and nothing after them.

tickets.hint: grep the beef out of the file, then pipe that into head -n 2.

after.text: See what head didn't get? A file. It took what grep handed it.

brief.text: Somebody circled the fifth thing on the menu and wrote NO. I need to know what I'm not washing up after. Just that one line.

tickets.hint: Take the first five lines, then pipe them on and keep only the last.

after.text: The first five, then the last of those. Two small tools, and you've built one that fetches line five.

brief.text: Three stations now. How many melts on the rail that aren't turkey? A number, Chef.

tickets.hint: Melts first, then drop the turkey, then count what's left. A pipe between each.

after.text: As many stations as you like. Each one only ever sees what the one before it plated.

outro.text: Fine. FINE. It's a good pass.
outro.say: Fine. Fine. It's a good pass.

outro.text: Don't you Chef me, I taught you to hold a knife. ...Chef.

intro.text: Mise en place, Chef. Everything in its place before service. That goes for lines of text too.
I put things in order. Nobody notices until I don't.
sort puts lines in order. uniq throws out repeats. There's a catch in each one, which is why we're doing this before the rush.
intro.say: sort puts lines in order. unique throws out repeats. There's a catch in each one, which is why we're doing this before the rush.

brief.text: Tonight's tabs. Put them in order, smallest first. And look out: sort reads like a dictionary unless you tell it these are numbers.

tickets.hint: sort alone puts 100 before 12. -n makes it read the numbers.

after.text: Without -n it goes letter by letter, and the letter 1 comes before the letter 8. So a hundred lands on top. It has caught everybody once.
after.say: Without dash N it goes letter by letter, and the letter 1 comes before the letter 8. So a hundred lands on top. It has caught everybody once.

brief.text: Smallest first? Who cares about the small ones! Show me the big spenders! Biggest at the top!

tickets.hint: Keep -n, and add -r to turn the order round.

after.text: -r for reverse. You can stack options like that, or squash them into one: -rn. Same thing.
after.say: dash R for reverse. You can stack options like that, or squash them into one: dash R N. Same thing.

brief.text: What did we actually sell tonight? Each thing once. Mind the catch: uniq only notices a repeat when it's right behind the one before.
brief.say: What did we actually sell tonight? Each thing once. Mind the catch: unique only notices a repeat when it's right behind the one before.

tickets.hint: Sort first, so the repeats stand together. Then pipe into uniq.

after.text: Line them up first. Then you can see which ones are the same. I do it with forks.

brief.text: Now the one the owner asks every night: how many of each? uniq can count the repeats as it drops them.
brief.say: Now the one the owner asks every night: how many of each? unique can count the repeats as it drops them.

tickets.hint: The same line as before, with -c on uniq.

after.text: sort, then uniq -c. Remember that pair, Chef. You'll be using it for the rest of your life.
after.say: sort, then unique dash C. Remember that pair, Chef. You'll be using it for the rest of your life.

shifts.title: The Critic
shifts.lesson: cut, tr, > and the whole line

intro.text: She's here! Table one! Regina Root, from the Lakeside Ledger!
What Root asks for, Root gets, Chef. Nobody in this town says no to Root.
I'm told this is the kitchen where nobody shouts. We shall see.
Tickets come off the machine with commas in them now: table, dish, how they want it. You're going to need a knife.

brief.text: Just the dishes, Chef: the second thing on every ticket. cut slices each line where you tell it to.

tickets.hint: cut, then -d, to split at the commas, then -f2 for the second piece.

after.text: -d is the delimiter: where to cut. -f is the field: which slice to keep.
after.say: dash D is the delimiter: where to cut. dash F is the field: which slice to keep.

brief.text: My specials board! A new pun every day for thirty years! Put it in capitals. She's a critic, she respects capitals!

tickets.hint: tr never opens a file. cat the board, and pipe it in.

after.text: tr swaps each character in the first list for its partner in the second. It only takes what comes down the pass, which is what cat is for.
after.say: T R swaps each character in the first list for its partner in the second. It only takes what comes down the pass, which is what cat is for.

brief.text: We're out of two things and she's about to order. Put every 86 on the board for me. On the board. Not out loud.
brief.say: We're out of two things and she's about to order. Put every eighty-six on the board for me. On the board. Not out loud.

tickets.hint: grep the 86s, then send them into the file with >.

after.text: On the board. Nothing said out loud. That's how I like it.

then.text: That arrow sends what a command prints into a file instead of to the pass. It wipes the file first, so mind where you point it.
The machine! The to-go machine! It won't stop printing!
then.say: [panicking] The machine! The to-go machine! It won't stop printing!

then.text: Twelve tickets and climbing. Don't read them, Chef. Build a line.
One question, Chef, and I'll have the answer on one line.

brief.text: Out of everything this kitchen has sent tonight: what do you sell the most of, and how many?

tickets.hint: Slice out the dishes, sort them, count each, sort the counts biggest first, keep the top line.

after.text: Fries. Five stations, not one raised voice, and the answer is fries.

outro.text: I have eaten in kitchens with forty cooks who could not have told me that.
The Standard Inn. Small tools, kept sharp, each doing one thing. I'll be back on Tuesday.
She's coming back! SHE'S COMING BACK!
outro.say: [shouting, overjoyed] She's coming back! She's coming back!

command.title: A command
command.text: A command is one short word that tells the kitchen to do one job. This one lists the files it has.

cat.title: Command, then file
cat.text: Most commands need to know what to work on. Put the file's name after the command, with a space between.
chips: read a file out, top to bottom

head.title: Options
head.text: An option is a dash and a letter after the command. It changes how the command does its job. Some take a value.
chips: the first lines of a file (ten, unless told)

wc.title: wc counts
wc.text: wc counts what's in a file: its lines, its words and its characters. An option picks just one of them.
wc.say: W C counts what's in a file: its lines, its words and its characters. An option picks just one of them.

grep.title: grep
grep.text: grep keeps the lines that have your word on them and drops the rest. The word comes first, then the file. Capitals count.
chips: keep only the lines that match

grep_options.title: Three ways to grep
grep_options.text: The same search, done three other ways.

pipe.title: The pipe
pipe.text: A pipe joins two commands. What the left one prints goes to the right one as its input, instead of to the screen.

sort.title: sort
sort.text: sort puts lines in order. On its own it sorts like a dictionary, so 100 comes before 12.

uniq.title: uniq
uniq.text: uniq drops a line that repeats the line just before it. Only just before: so sort first, and the repeats stand together.
uniq.say: unique drops a line that repeats the line just before it. Only just before: so sort first, and the repeats stand together.

cut.title: cut
cut.text: cut keeps one slice of every line. Tell it where the lines split, and which piece you want.

tr.title: tr
tr.text: tr swaps characters: each one in the first list becomes its partner in the second. It reads only what's piped in.
tr.say: T R swaps characters: each one in the first list becomes its partner in the second. It reads only what's piped in.
chips: every small letter, a to z

redirect.title: Into a file
redirect.text: > sends what a command prints into a file instead of to the screen. The file is wiped, then written.
redirect.say: The arrow sends what a command prints into a file instead of to the screen. The file is wiped, then written.

glossary.ls: list the files in the kitchen
glossary.cat: read files out, top to bottom
glossary.head: the first lines (ten, unless told)
glossary.grep: keep the lines that match a word
glossary.cut: keep one slice of every line
glossary.|: pass the output to the next command
glossary.-n: by number, not letter by letter
glossary.a-z: every small letter, a to z
glossary.> file: write the output into this file
glossary.grep melt orders.txt: the orders with melt on them

nothing: Nothing reached the pass, Chef. The ticket starts with "{want}".
The pass is empty. I'm looking for "{want}".
order: Right plates, wrong order. I got "{got}" where the ticket says "{want}".
It's all there, Chef, just not in that order. "{want}" goes where "{got}" is.
extra: Too much food. "{got}" isn't on the ticket.
short: The ticket says "{want}" too. It never reached the pass.
wrong: Line {n}: you sent "{got}". The ticket says "{want}".
I've got "{got}" on the pass. The ticket wants "{want}".
tofile: That came out loud, Chef. The ticket wants it written into {file}.
It's on the pass. It should be in {file}.
infile: Nothing reached the pass: it all went into {file}. This ticket wants it out here.
You wrote it down in {file}, Chef. I need it on the pass.
par: Clean. Not a wasted word on that line.
That's the shortest line there is. Yes, Chef.
Tight. I couldn't take a chip off that.
over: It works. There's a shorter line, if you ever want to show off.
That'll do. Longer than it needs to be, but the plate's right.

errors.empty: Nothing on the line, Chef. I can't fire nothing.
errors.notfound: The first word has to be a command, and the shell doesn't know one called {token}.
errors.nofile: There's no file called {token} in this kitchen.
errors.waiting: {token} is standing at its station with nothing coming down the line. Give it a file, or pipe something in.
errors.pipe_start: A pipe needs a command on its left to take from.
errors.pipe_end: A pipe needs a command on its right to hand to.
errors.redirect: That arrow needs a file to point at.
errors.number: That wants a number of lines, and {token} isn't one.
errors.usage: grep needs to be told what to look for.
errors.extra: One thing too many on that command: {token}.
errors.nolist: cut needs to know which piece to keep. Give it an -f.
errors.delimiter: cut can only split at one single character.
errors.list: That isn't a piece cut can count to.
errors.tr_operand: tr swaps one list of characters for another. It needs both lists.
errors.tr_extra: tr never opens a file, so {token} is one word too many. Pipe the file in.
errors.unsupported: That's real shell, but nobody has taught it in this kitchen yet. Stick to the cards, Chef.
errors.clobber: That line reads a file while it's writing over it. Don't, Chef. It ends in tears.
